pos: n. (Rudolf Gwalther, 1519–1586, Zwingli's son-in-law and Bullinger's successor as chief pastor of Zurich)
etymology: German Rudolf, famous wolf, from Germanic hrod and wulf; Gwalther, a Swiss form of Walter, ruler of the army.
biblical_def: Rudolf Gwalther was brought up in Bullinger's household after Kappel, married Zwingli's daughter Regula, and so stood by blood and by marriage at the centre of the Zurich church for sixty years. He studied at Basel, Strasbourg, Lausanne and Oxford, translated Zwingli's Latin works into German and his German works into Latin, and published the Archetypae homiliarum, complete sets of model homilies on the New Testament books that gave hard-pressed country pastors something sound to preach from. When Bullinger died in 1575 Gwalther succeeded him as antistes and held the office eleven years, keeping Zurich steady through the hardening of the Lutheran-Reformed division and corresponding with the English bishops and the persecuted of France. He was the third man in a single unbroken line — Zwingli, Bullinger, Gwalther — and his part was to hand on what the first two had built. “One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts” (Psa 145:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a homily as a sermon or discourse on a point of doctrine, and succession as a following in order, the act of taking another's place.
webster_full: HOM'ILY, n. A discourse or sermon read or pronounced to an audience; a plain discourse on a point of doctrine.
SUCCES'SION, n. A following of things in order; the act of taking the place of another in office.
AN'TISTES, n. A presiding minister; in the Swiss churches, the chief pastor of a city.
DECLARE', v. To make known; to tell explicitly; to publish; to proclaim.
scriptures: One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts.

And it came to pass, when they were gone over, that Elijah said unto Elisha, Ask what I shall do for thee, before I be taken away from thee. And Elisha said, I pray thee, let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me.

I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
corruption_summary: The third man of the Zurich line, who wrote homilies for country pastors.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the suspicion attaching to printed sermon helps. Gwalther's homilies were written because many rural Zurich pastors had little Latin and no library, and the choice before them was a sound model or nothing. The abuse of such books by lazy men is real; it is not an argument against providing them for able men who are poor.

The principle to recover is that succession in the church is a succession in doctrine and labour rather than in office alone. Elisha asked for the thing itself and not the mantle only — “let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me” (2Ki 2:9) — and the promise made to Joshua as he took up Moses's work is the promise every successor needs: “as I was with Moses, so I will be with thee: I will not fail thee, nor forsake thee” (Jos 1:5).

pos: n. (Josias Simler, 1530–1576, Zurich professor of theology and biographer of the Reformers)
etymology: Hebrew Yoshiyahu, the LORD supports, through Josias; Simler, a Swiss family name.
biblical_def: Josias Simler was the son of a Zurich pastor, brought up partly in Bullinger's house, and from 1560 professor of theology in the Zurich school, where he lectured on the Old Testament and wrote commentaries on Exodus and the Gospels. His lasting service was of another kind. He wrote the lives of the men he had known — Peter Martyr Vermigli, Heinrich Bullinger, the naturalist Conrad Gesner, his own father-in-law — promptly, carefully, and from the papers and the testimony of those still living, and most of what later ages know of the second Zurich generation rests on his work. He also edited Vermigli's Loci Communes, which carried Reformed theology across Europe in a usable form. He was dead at forty-six of the gout that had crippled him for years. The church owes him the unglamorous debt it owes every faithful recorder: without him the Zurich Reformation would be a set of conclusions without faces. “by it he being dead yet speaketh” (Heb 11:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines biography as the history of the life and character of a particular person, and memory as the remembrance of a person or thing.
webster_full: BIOG'RAPHY, n. The history of the life and character of a particular person.
MEM'ORY, n. The faculty of the mind by which it retains knowledge; remembrance; the reputation of one deceased.
COM'MONPLACES, n. In theology, the chief heads or topics of doctrine, treated in order.
RECORD'ER, n. One whose official duty is to register writings or transactions.

corruption_summary: The Zurich professor who wrote down the lives of the men he had known.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern suspicion of the memorial life as a genre: because Simler admired his subjects, his lives are discounted as hagiography. He was writing within a few years of the deaths, for readers who had known the men, and his biographies can be checked against the surviving correspondence; where they have been, they stand up.

The principle to recover is that remembering the faithful is commanded and useful, and that the use is imitation rather than sentiment: “That ye be not slothful, but followers of them who through faith and patience inherit the promises” (Heb 6:12). Solomon states the plain contrast that makes such recording worth a lifetime: “The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot” (Pro 10:7).

pos: n. (Johann Jakob Breitinger, 1575–1645, antistes of Zurich, delegate to the Synod of Dort)
etymology: German Johann, the LORD is gracious; Jakob, from Hebrew Yaaqob, he takes by the heel; Breitinger, of the broad meadow.
biblical_def: Johann Jakob Breitinger was antistes of Zurich from 1613 until his death in 1645, thirty-two years that covered the whole of the Thirty Years' War. He was Zurich's delegate to the Synod of Dort in 1618 and voted with the strictest party against the Remonstrants. At home he was a disciplinarian in the old Zwinglian mould: he pressed the magistrates year after year against the mercenary trade by which Swiss cantons sold their young men to foreign armies for pensions, against the luxury of the patrician houses, and against the slackness of the country clergy, and he carried a reform of the church ordinances and of the schools. He organised relief and asylum for the Protestants of the Grisons and of the Palatinate when the war broke over them. His reputation is of a severe man, and he was; the severity was spent on the sins of his own ruling class rather than on the poor. “Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel” (Eze 3:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mercenary as a soldier who serves for pay in foreign service, and a watchman as one set to guard and give warning.
webster_full: MER'CENARY, n. One who is hired; a soldier who is hired into foreign service.
WATCH'MAN, n. A sentinel; a guard; one set to watch and give notice of danger.
DIS'CIPLINE, n. Correction; chastisement; the exercise of government over members of a church.
LUX'URY, n. A free or extravagant indulgence in the pleasures of the table or of dress.
scriptures: Eze 3:17
Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel: therefore hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me.
Them that sin rebuke before all, that others also may fear.
Tit 2:12
Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world;
Pro 1:19
So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof.
corruption_summary: Thirty-two years against the mercenary trade and the luxury of the patricians.
corruption_paragraphs: Breitinger is the standing example used to argue that the Reformed pastorate was a machinery of social control, forever regulating dress, drink and amusement. The charge needs its direction restored. The discipline he pressed hardest was against the men who ran the city: the pension-takers who sold Swiss recruits to Catholic France and Spain, and the patricians whose houses were full while the refugees from the Grisons starved. A clergy that scolds the powerful is not an instrument of the powerful.

The principle to recover is that rebuke is to be public where the sin is public and the sinner prominent: “Them that sin rebuke before all, that others also may fear” (1Ti 5:20). And the trade he set himself against is named in Proverbs with its own penalty attached: “So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof” (Pro 1:19).

pos: n. (Ludwig Lavater, 1527–1586, Zurich pastor, commentator and historian of the eucharistic controversy)
etymology: German Ludwig, famous in battle, from Germanic hlud and wig; Lavater, a Zurich family name.
biblical_def: Ludwig Lavater married Bullinger's daughter, served Zurich churches for thirty years, and became archdeacon of the Great Minster. He wrote commentaries on Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Proverbs, Ezekiel and Joshua, and a history of the controversy over the Lord's Supper that is still a source for the Zurich side of it. He is best remembered, however, for a small book of 1569 on spectres and apparitions, which gathered the reports and the classical and medieval authorities and then applied the Reformed doctrine to them: that the dead do not return, that what the living meet is either a natural deception or a devil, and that the whole machinery of purgatory and of appearing souls which the medieval church had built on such stories is therefore groundless. It was translated into English in 1572 and read for a century. A pastor answering his people's night fears out of the Scriptures is doing the work, not indulging a curiosity. “should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?” (Isa 8:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a spectre as an apparition, the appearance of a person who is dead, and necromancy as the pretended art of revealing future events by communication with the dead.
webster_full: SPEC'TRE, n. An apparition; the appearance of a person who is dead; a ghost.
NECROMAN'CY, n. The pretended art of revealing future events by communication with the dead; conjuration.
PUR'GATORY, n. A supposed place in which souls are purified by fire from carnal impurities.
APPARI'TION, n. The thing appearing; a ghost; a spectre; a visible spirit.
scriptures: Isa 8:19
And when they shall say unto you, Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?
Regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards, to be defiled by them: I am the LORD your God.
Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have.
Ecc 9:5

corruption_summary: The Zurich pastor who answered ghost stories out of Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: The traffic Lavater wrote against has never stopped, and in our own day it is bigger than it was in his. Mediums, channelling, the whole industry of contact with the departed, and the softer domestic version in which a dead relative is said to be present and watching, all rest on the premise Scripture forbids: that the living may deal with the dead. The modern form is gentler in tone and identical in substance, and it does the same two injuries, trading on grief and displacing the God who alone is to be sought.

The principle to recover is the prohibition with its reason, which is not that such dealings never produce anything but that they are a defilement and a desertion: “Regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards, to be defiled by them: I am the LORD your God” (Lev 19:31). Isaiah puts the absurdity of it as a question: “should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?” (Isa 8:19).

pos: n. (Leo Jud, 1482–1542, pastor at St Peter's in Zurich, Zwingli's closest colleague and chief translator)
etymology: Latin Leo, a lion; Jud, an Alsatian family name, latinised by him as Judae.
biblical_def: Leo Jud was an Alsatian who met Zwingli as a fellow student at Basel and remained the nearest man to him for the rest of Zwingli's life. He followed him to Einsiedeln and then, in 1523, to Zurich, where he was pastor of St Peter's for nineteen years. He was the workhorse of the Zurich Reformation and preferred it that way: he translated the greater part of Zwingli's Latin writings into German and his German into Latin, rendered Augustine and Chrysostom and Erasmus for German readers, did the Apocrypha for the Zurich Bible, helped produce the Latin version of the Old Testament that bears Zurich's name, and wrote the two catechisms by which Zurich children were taught. He died in 1542, a year before the catechism was printed. The Reformation is usually told through the men who stood up in the disputations; it was carried by men like Jud, who sat in a study turning other men's books into a language that could be read. “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour” (Ecc 4:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a colleague as a partner or associate in office, and to translate as to interpret, to render into another language.
webster_full: COL'LEAGUE, n. A partner or associate in the same office, employment or commission.
TRANSLA'TE, v. To interpret; to render into another language; to express the sense in other words.
LIKE'MINDED, a. Having a like disposition or purpose.
FEL'LOWWORKER, n. One engaged in the same labour or occupation with another.
scriptures: Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.

corruption_summary: Zwingli's closest colleague, who spent his life translating other men's books.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the habit of reading a man like Jud as a subordinate rather than a colleague — an assistant to Zwingli, with his own catechisms and translations treated as service work. The Zurich Bible and the Zurich catechisms are not service work; they are what the people of that canton actually held in their hands.

The principle to recover is that the ministry is given in company and that the companion's part is not a lesser calling. Paul names the scarcity of such men as a grief — “For I have no man likeminded, who will naturally care for your state” (Php 2:20) — and he records the few who stood by him with evident gratitude: “These only are my fellowworkers unto the kingdom of God, which have been a comfort unto me” (Col 4:11).

pos: n. (Konrad Pellikan, 1478–1556, Franciscan Hebraist, professor of Hebrew at Zurich, author of the first Christian Hebrew grammar in Germany)
etymology: German Konrad, bold counsel, from Germanic kuoni and rad; Pellikan, a grecised rendering of his family name Kurschner, a furrier.
biblical_def: Konrad Pellikan taught himself Hebrew as a young Franciscan with almost nothing to work from — a borrowed Hebrew Bible, a few pages of grammar in a Latin book, and the help of a converted Jew he met once — and in 1504, at twenty-six, published De modo legendi et intelligendi Hebraeum, the first Hebrew grammar written by a Christian in Germany and printed four years before Reuchlin's. He rose to be provincial of his order, left it for the evangelical faith in 1526, and spent the last thirty years of his life as professor of Hebrew at Zurich, where he worked on the Zurich Bible, lectured on the Old Testament, built the library, and wrote a commentary on the whole of Scripture. He also catalogued the Zurich manuscripts and left an autobiography that is one of the best accounts of a scholar's life in that century. The Reformation's recovery of the Old Testament rested on men who first had to construct the means of reading it. “unto them were committed the oracles of God” (Rom 3:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a grammar as the art of speaking or writing a language with propriety, and an oracle as the communications of God to the prophets.
webster_full: GRAM'MAR, n. The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety; a book containing its principles.
OR'ACLE, n. The communications, revelations or messages delivered by God to prophets; the Scriptures.
HE'BRAIST, n. One versed in the Hebrew language.
LI'BRARY, n. A collection of books belonging to a private person or to a public institution.

corruption_summary: The Franciscan who taught himself Hebrew and wrote Germany its first grammar.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a quiet neglect of the Old Testament in Protestant preaching, which makes the labour of men like Pellikan look like antiquarian specialism. He did not learn Hebrew to be a specialist. He learned it because three-quarters of the Bible is written in it and the church of his day could not read them.

The principle to recover is that the Old Testament is Christian Scripture and testifies of Christ, so that a church without Hebrew is a church with a closed quarter of its own book. The Lord puts Moses and the prophets in the place of sufficient testimony — “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them” (Luk 16:29) — and states the matter about Moses directly: “for he wrote of me” (Joh 5:46).

pos: n. (Theodor Bibliander, 1509–1564, Zwingli's successor in the Old Testament chair at Zurich, orientalist and editor of the first printed Qur'an)
etymology: Greek Theodoros, gift of God; Bibliander, a grecised form of his family name Buchmann, book-man.
biblical_def: Theodor Bibliander studied Hebrew under Pellikan and succeeded Zwingli in the Zurich chair of Old Testament in 1532, holding it for twenty-eight years. He was the first systematic comparative linguist of the age, publishing in 1548 a treatise comparing the grammar of the Semitic and other tongues; and in 1543 he brought out at Basel, after the city magistrates had imprisoned him for attempting it and Luther had written urging that it be allowed, the first printed edition of the Qur'an in Latin, with the argument that Christians cannot answer a religion they have not read. He was also one of the gentlest men of his century, and it cost him his chair. He resisted the hardening of the Zurich doctrine of predestination under Peter Martyr Vermigli's influence, holding to a more universal view of the offer of the gospel, and was pensioned off in 1560. The dictionary holds Zurich's doctrine and records Bibliander's principle on the Qur'an as sound. “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear” (1Pe 3:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an apology as a defence or vindication, and an orientalist as one versed in the eastern languages.
webster_full: APOL'OGY, n. A defence or justification of what appears to others wrong; a vindication.
O'RIENTALIST, n. An inhabitant of the eastern parts of the world; one versed in eastern languages.
MEEK'NESS, n. Softness of temper; mildness; gentleness; forbearance under injuries.
COMPAR'ATIVE, a. Estimated by comparison; having the power of comparing.

(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
corruption_summary: The orientalist who printed the Qur'an so Christians could answer it.
corruption_paragraphs: Bibliander is now enlisted on both sides of a modern quarrel. He is cited as a pioneer of interfaith respect, as though his purpose in printing the Qur'an had been appreciation; and he is cited by others as proof that studying a false religion is the first step to excusing it. His own preface settles it: he printed the book so that its errors could be shown from its own pages, and he thought Christians disgraced themselves by refuting from rumour what they had never read.

The principle to recover is that an answer must be informed and civil without being soft: “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear” (1Pe 3:15). Solomon states the rule Bibliander was applying to Islam and his opponents were breaking: “He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him” (Pro 18:13).

pos: n. (the Swiss city and canton on the Rhine, reformed in 1529)
etymology: German, probably Schiffhausen, the boat-houses, from the Rhine portage above the falls where cargo had to be unloaded.
biblical_def: Schaffhausen stands on the right bank of the Rhine above the great falls, the one Swiss canton wholly north of the river, and in the sixteenth century it was a free imperial city dominated by the Benedictine abbey of All Saints. Sebastian Hofmeister, a native, brought the evangelical cause home from the Zurich disputations in 1523 and carried much of the town; the council wavered under pressure from the Catholic cantons and expelled him in 1525, and for four more years the city hung between. In 1529, in the wave that followed Bern, the council abolished the mass, removed the images, and dissolved the abbey, applying its revenues to the school and to the poor. Schaffhausen then subscribed the First Helvetic Confession of 1536 and the Second of 1566 and has been Reformed since. Its history is a useful corrective to any account of the Swiss Reformation as a sudden municipal decision: here it took six years, one expulsion and two reversals. “Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid” (Mat 5:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a canton as a small territory or clan constituting a distinct state, and an abbey as a monastery governed by an abbot.
webster_full: CAN'TON, n. A small portion of territory constituting a distinct government, as in Switzerland.
AB'BEY, n. A monastery or society of persons of either sex, governed by an abbot or abbess.
RE'VENUE, n. The annual rents, profits, interest or issues of any species of property.
IM'PERIAL CITY, A free city of the Empire, subject to the emperor alone.

corruption_summary: The Rhine city that took six years and two reversals to reform.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the tidy narrative: the Swiss Reformation presented as a series of clean council votes, city by city, as though a magistracy heard the arguments and decided. Schaffhausen expelled its reformer in 1525 and reformed without him in 1529, and in between it was pulled back and forth by its neighbours' threats and its abbey's money.

The principle to recover is that a city's standing is a moral thing and its safety is not in its walls: “By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted: but it is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked” (Pro 11:11). Isaiah states what a reformed commonwealth is promised and what it is to be called: “afterward thou shalt be called, The city of righteousness, the faithful city” (Isa 1:26).

pos: n. (the Swiss city and canton, reformed in 1527 while its abbey remained Roman)
etymology: Named for the Irish monk Gallus, a companion of Columbanus, whose hermitage of about 612 became the great abbey.
biblical_def: St Gallen grew up around the abbey founded on the hermitage of the Irish monk Gallus, and by the sixteenth century the abbey was one of the richest in Europe and the town beneath it a linen-weaving city that had bought most of its liberties. The two reformed differently, and that is the point of the entry. Under Joachim Vadian as mayor and with the preaching of Johannes Kessler and others, the town abolished the mass in 1527, cleared the images from its churches, and took the Reformed confession. The abbey never did. The abbot kept his lands and his Roman worship, withdrew, returned with the Catholic cantons' backing after Kappel in 1531, and abbey and town lived side by side in one valley, under separate religions and separate governments, until the French swept the arrangement away in 1798. A Reformed city and a Benedictine abbey within one wall's sight for two hundred and seventy years is an instructive thing. “And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives” (Jer 29:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an abbot as the superior of a monastery, and a burgh as a corporate town or borough.
webster_full: AB'BOT, n. The superior or governor of an abbey or monastery.
BURGH, n. A borough; a corporate town or village with certain privileges.
HER'MITAGE, n. The habitation of a hermit; a cell or dwelling in a solitary place.
DIVI'SION, n. The act of dividing; separation; disunion; discord.
scriptures: Jer 29:7
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
Think not that I am come to send peace on earth: I came not to send peace, but a sword.
Peace be within thy walls, and prosperity within thy palaces.
Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.
corruption_summary: A Reformed town and a Benedictine abbey in one valley for two hundred and seventy years.
corruption_paragraphs: St Gallen is the favourite exhibit for the view that the confessional divisions of the Reformation were about property and jurisdiction and could have been managed indefinitely without anyone being troubled about doctrine, since abbey and town did exactly that for nearly three centuries. The arrangement proves less than it seems. It held because both parties were armed, watched by powerful neighbours, and bound by treaties after a civil war; and it coexisted with real and continuing disagreement about how a sinner is saved.

The principle to recover is that Christians seek the peace of the city they live in while refusing to purchase it with the truth. Jeremiah's command to the exiles is positive and unqualified — “and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace” (Jer 29:7) — and the Lord's own word keeps the other half in view: “I came not to send peace, but a sword” (Mat 10:34).

pos: n. (Robert Estienne, 1503–1559, royal printer of Paris and then of Geneva, who divided the Bible into verses)
etymology: French Robert, bright fame, from Germanic hrod and beraht; Estienne, French form of Stephen, latinised Stephanus.
biblical_def: Robert Estienne was the greatest printer of his century and the man whose decisions still govern how every Christian cites Scripture. Royal printer at Paris in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, he produced critical editions of the Vulgate, four Greek New Testaments, Hebrew Bibles, and the Thesaurus linguae latinae that founded modern Latin lexicography. The Sorbonne harried him for the notes in his Bibles until in 1550 he left for Geneva, became a citizen, joined the Reformed church, and printed for Calvin and Beza for the rest of his life. His fourth Greek New Testament of 1551 was the first to carry the division of the chapters into numbered verses, and his 1553 French Bible and 1555 Latin Vulgate extended the numbering to the whole canon; it was adopted everywhere within a generation and has never been displaced. The convenience is so complete that it has become invisible: every reference in this dictionary and in every other depends on a Paris printer's decision made in flight. “and began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus” (Act 8:35).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a verse as a short division of any composition, particularly of the chapters of Scripture, and a thesaurus as a treasury or repository.
webster_full: VERSE, n. A short division of any composition; a line; in the Scriptures, one of the short divisions of a chapter.
THESAU'RUS, n. A treasury; a repository, as of words or of knowledge.
PRINT'ER, n. One that prints books, pamphlets or papers.
LEXICOG'RAPHY, n. The act of writing a lexicon or dictionary; the art of defining words.
scriptures: Act 8:35
Then Philip opened his mouth, and began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus.
Luk 4:17
And there was delivered unto him the book of the prophet Esaias. And when he had opened the book, he found the place where it was written,
Act 8:32
The place of the scripture which he read was this, He was led as a sheep to the slaughter; and like a lamb dumb before his shearer, so opened he not his mouth:
But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name.
corruption_summary: The printer who numbered the verses, and fled Paris for Geneva.
corruption_paragraphs: A modern objection to Estienne's verses deserves a hearing and a limit. The numbering, it is said, atomises Scripture: readers quote single verses out of their paragraphs, preachers build on fragments, and whole arguments like Romans 9 are chopped into mottoes. The complaint is fair against a vice, not against the tool. Chapter and verse make a text citable, checkable and memorisable, and the discipline of reading in context is a duty that no numbering scheme can either impose or prevent.

The principle to recover is that Scripture is to be located and handled precisely, which is what a reference is for. Philip does not preach in general; he begins at the place the eunuch was reading — “and began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus” (Act 8:35) — and the Lord in the Nazareth synagogue “found the place where it was written” (Luk 4:17). Estienne's numbers simply make finding the place a thing any reader can do.
